abstract: Each legume plant in the field typically hosts several strains of rhizobia, yet plant benefits from different strains are often compared using single-strain experiments. We present an automated protocol to track nodule growth (using photos and the RootPainter model) and to measure hydrogen production, a nondestructive proxy for nitrogen fixation. Soybean seed yield was highly correlated with hydrogen production (integrated over growth), except in 5 of 20 field isolates of rhizobia, apparent hydrogen recyclers. Most yield differences among strains were due to differences in nodule mass per plant, which might not predict field benefits, rather than benefit per nodule mass. However, three isolates with the greatest nodule mass provided the least yield benefit. Strain rankings were mostly consistent in a second experiment, but two exceptions showed the value of replication. For ten of 12 strains in the second experiment, final seed weight was highly correlated with week-6 estimates of shoot weight, but two exceptions suggest that vegetative growth may not always predict fitness benefits to plants. Although singly-inoculated plants are an imperfect proxy for multiply-infected plants in the field, tracking nodule growth and measuring hydrogen production can make these experiments more informative.
